processing: Suited to northern Fujian (Minbei) oolong processing. A 2023 study found light tossing gives a tight, fresh tasting tea, while heavier tossing gives a mellower cup with more prominent florals.
harvest_season: A late-budding cultivar, so its spring picking comes after that of early varieties; exact dates vary with place.
appearance_dry: Tightly formed strips when lightly tossed, in the dark tone usual for Minbei oolong.
appearance_liquor: A clear golden orange, as is usual for Minbei-style oolong.
appearance_wet: Small leaves, as expected from a small-leaf cultivar, with reddened edges typical of oolong.
taste_profile: Lightly tossed tea tastes fresh and brisk; heavier tossing gives a thicker, mellower cup with more prominent florals.

brewing.notes: A general oolong starting point, not one set for this cultivar. Use a porcelain gaiwan to show the florals and keep early steeps short.

vintage_note: Rarely seen as a named tea on the open market. Like other Fujian oolongs it would normally be sold by the current year's harvest; ask whether the lot was lightly or heavily tossed, since that decides the style.
description:
Chungui is a modern oolong cultivar, not a historic named tea. It was selected from natural hybrid offspring of Huang Dan, the fragrant Anxi cultivar, in work published by Fujian researchers. It is a late-budding shrub with small leaves.

Trials found it suits northern Fujian oolong making, and that the amount of tossing changes the tea a good deal. Light tossing keeps the leaf tight with a fresh taste, while heavier tossing builds a mellower cup and brings the florals forward.

Brew it as you would other Minbei oolongs, in a gaiwan with very hot water and short first steeps. Published notes are limited to the floral and fresh character above, so taste it without expecting a set profile.

You are more likely to meet the name in growers' and researchers' notes than on a shop shelf. If you do find a lot, ask for the year and how heavily it was tossed.
history: Chungui was bred by single-plant selection from natural hybrid offspring of Huang Dan, and a paper on it appeared in the Fujian Journal of Agricultural Sciences in 2017, reporting trials from 2002 to 2014. That work recommends it for Fu'an and areas with a similar climate. Little else is documented about its spread or commercial use.
